claims.text: Configurational entropy controls the premelting and melting behavior of high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy suppresses elemental segregation at nanoparticle surfaces.
Homogeneous atomic mixing reduces surface diffusion.
Reduced surface diffusion delays formation of a liquid-like premelting layer.
Suppressed segregation elevates the effective melting temperature relative to nanoparticles in which segregation is promoted.
The initial nanoparticles are equiatomic, 10–100 nm in size, and have a random homogeneous distribution of multiple metals.
Post-synthesis heat treatment can induce partial elemental segregation and thereby reduce configurational disorder relative to the as-synthesized particles.
High-vacuum or inert-atmosphere heating minimizes oxidation and other extrinsic effects.
The degree of atomic mixing or segregation at nanoparticle surfaces and interfaces influences surface energy and atomic mobility.
Compositionally enriched nanoparticle shells or interfaces can occur in a nanostructured high-entropy alloy.
High configurational entropy produces a uniform atomic distribution that kinetically impedes surface-atom diffusion.
Elemental segregation locally concentrates lower-melting constituents and thereby lowers the local melting point.
Lower local melting points caused by segregation promote earlier nanoparticle premelting.
Melting behavior is governed by a balance between entropy-driven mixing and enthalpy-driven segregation.
As-synthesized equiatomic particles will show later surface-premelting onset and a higher complete melting temperature than heat-treated segregated particles.
The predicted trend should hold for particles approximately 10–100 nm in size.
The mechanism should hold when mixing enthalpy is near zero or only modestly positive.
Strong segregation tendencies, particle sizes outside 10–100 nm, and rapid-heating-dependent surface or bulk diffusion may cause deviations from the prediction.
TEM, DSC, and surface-compositional analysis can compare premelting onset, complete melting temperature, and segregation between the two particle sets.
Failure of the homogeneous particles to show delayed premelting and higher melting temperature, including indistinguishable behavior between groups, would falsify the hypothesis.
